title: Zephyrine and the Undertow
premise: After his mother's funeral, Theo Winterbourne finds a cache of unsent letters behind her wardrobe—letters addressed to a woman named Zephyrine in the old riverside neighborhood the family fled decades ago. Reading them, Theo uncovers the betrayal that bought the family's respectability: his mother informed on Zephyrine's brother to protect her husband's business, then spent forty years paying for it in silence. As developers prepare to raze the old neighborhood, Theo travels there against his father's wishes, meets Zephyrine's surviving daughter, and must choose between preserving the family's carefully arranged lie and telling a truth that will shatter it. The book ends with Theo reading the final letter aloud at the neighborhood's last community meeting, severing himself from his inheritance but finally, truly belonging to someone.
about_author: Sebastian Okonkwo is a former archivist who spent six years cataloging the unclaimed letters of a decommissioned postal depot, an experience that taught him how much of a life can fit inside an envelope. He writes from a rented room above a shuttered laundrette, where he is at work on a second novel about families that mistake silence for peace.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. In the week after the funeral, Theo manages mourners with practiced charm while cataloging his mother's immaculate, unreadable house. A wardrobe moved by movers reveals a shoebox of letters, all addressed to Zephyrine, none ever posted. Theo reads the first one and recognizes, with dread, his mother's handwriting at its most alive. Emotional beat: grief curdling into suspicion—the first crack in the family's polished surface.

chapters.title: Forty Years of Unsent Weather
chapters.summary: Alternating Theo's present-day POV with excerpts from the letters themselves. The letters trace a deep friendship ruptured by an unnamed act; Theo pieces together that his mother reported Zephyrine's brother to authorities to shield his father's dealings. His father, sensing discovery, warns Theo to burn the box 'for everyone's sake.' Emotional beat: rising tension as loyalty to the living collides with fidelity to the dead.

chapters.title: The Last Bus to Saltmarsh Row
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Defying his father, Theo rides the soon-to-be-rerouted bus to the condemned neighborhood and finds Amara, Zephyrine's daughter, packing up her mother's flat. She knows half the story and hates the Winterbournes for the other half. Their charged, wary conversations become something like intimacy. When his father arrives to drag him home, Theo refuses publicly. Emotional beat: climax—love against duty, chosen in front of witnesses.

chapters.title: What the Tide Returns
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, closing at the neighborhood's final community meeting before demolition. He reads his mother's last letter aloud—her confession, her apology, her love—and lets the room do what rooms do with truth. His father disowns him; Amara takes his hand anyway. Theo walks out lighter than he arrived, carrying nothing but the box. Emotional beat: resolution through rupture—truth costs everything except the self.
